content.p: At about 1:40 p.m. on Friday 15 March 2019, a gunman began shooting worshippers at the Al Noor Mosque in Christchurch. Within ten minutes, according to New Zealand Police, 51 people had been shot dead at two mosques and 89 more wounded. The attacker was arrested at 1:50 p.m. by two officers who rammed his car. It was the worst terrorist attack in New Zealand's history.

The man responsible, Brenton Harrison Tarrant, a 29-year-old Australian, first pleaded not guilty and then, in March 2020, admitted 51 murders, 40 attempted murders and one charge of committing a terrorist act. On 27 August 2020 a High Court judge sentenced him to life imprisonment without parole, a sentence New Zealand had never before imposed. A Royal Commission of Inquiry later found that no information available to public agencies could have warned them of his plan, but criticised the way the security services had allocated their attention and the way firearms were licensed.

Tarrant travelled from Dunedin on the morning of the attack. Sentencing remarks published by the High Court record that he chose a Friday because he knew a large congregation would gather, and that he went to Christchurch intending to kill as many worshippers as he could. He carried firearms and incendiary devices and wore a helmet with a camera that streamed to an online audience. NPR reported that the stream ran for 17 minutes on Facebook before it was removed.

Only minutes before he began, according to the judge, Tarrant sent a document he called a manifesto to an extremist website, and emailed threats and the same document to the government and to media organisations. The judge said those messages gave the authorities no chance to intervene. The ideology behind the attack was, in the judge's words, "readily apparent": Tarrant had written references to the Crusades and to earlier terror attacks on his weapons, along with symbols that included those of the Nazi SS.

The two mosques were attacked in turn. At Al Noor, on Deans Avenue, the police museum account says 113 people were gathered for prayers, while the court estimated that about 190 worshippers were present; the sources do not explain the difference. The congregation was mostly men of various ages but included women and children. According to the sentencing remarks, the gunman killed people at the entrance and in the corridor, entered the main prayer room, where more than 120 people had heard the gunfire and moved toward the corners, and then fired into groups of people who could not escape. He left the building, shot at people trying to flee in the street, and returned.

The judge named many of those he killed. They included a three-year-old boy, Mucaad Ibrahim, who was clinging to his father's leg, and a 16-year-old, Hamza Alhaj Mustafa, who had escaped from the prayer room and sheltered behind parked cars. Two other people outside the mosque, a man and his four-year-old daughter, were seriously wounded.

The gunman then drove to the Linwood Islamic Centre on Linwood Avenue and attacked people in a car and in the driveway before entering the building and killing worshippers there. According to the court, he meant to drive on to Ashburton to attack a third mosque. His car was forced off the road by a police vehicle before he could.
content.h2: People who stood in the way
content.p: The police museum has recorded the acts of bravery that day. At Al Noor, Dr Naeem Rashid ran directly at the gunman and knocked him to the ground; he was shot dead, but his action, the police account says, let at least seven others escape. Hussein Al-Umari, a worshipper, walked toward the sound of the shots and turned to face the gunman in the prayer room, drawing attention from those who fled. He was mortally wounded and was awarded the New Zealand Bravery Star posthumously. Ziyaad Shah shielded another man with his own body and was wounded, and Zulfirman Syah shielded his son Averroes, with both of them wounded.

At Linwood, the sentencing remarks and the police account both single out Abdul Aziz Wahabzadah. He challenged the gunman at close range, threw a discarded firearm at the departing vehicle and chased it down Linwood Avenue. Back on Deans Avenue outside Al Noor, the police museum account says passing motorists, among them Carl Pomare, Mark Miller, Liam Beale and Lance Bradford, stopped to help the wounded. Pomare and Miller entered the line of fire to drag victims to safety, and Bradford stopped people who did not know what was happening from walking into the danger zone.

Senior Constables Scott Carmody and Jim Manning spotted the gunman's car among heavy traffic on Brougham Street. According to the police account, they believed they might be facing several shooters. They manoeuvred their patrol car to disable his vehicle and got him out of it within seconds. One officer found a large incendiary device in the rear of the car while the other kept his weapon on the man. Fearing he was reaching for a detonator inside his vest, Carmody knocked him unconscious with the butt of his rifle and handcuffed him. Both officers received the New Zealand Bravery Decoration. The court said Tarrant offered no resistance and was anxious not to be shot. He told police he had gone to both mosques to kill as many people as possible.

Tarrant was charged with murder and terrorism and initially pleaded not guilty. In March 2020 he abruptly changed his plea to guilty on all counts. Before sentencing he dismissed his lawyers and said he would represent himself; Pip Hall, a standby lawyer, told the court on the last day that Tarrant did not oppose a sentence of life without parole. The court restricted reporting of the proceedings because it feared he might use them as a platform for extremist ideology, according to Gulf News.

The hearing ran from 24 to 27 August 2020 in the Christchurch High Court. The judge received more than 200 victim impact statements, and 90 survivors and relatives spoke in person. Some addressed Tarrant angrily and called him a monster or a coward; a few said they forgave him. Ambreen Naeem, whose husband and son were killed, said she had never had a proper night's sleep since. Sara Qasem remembered her father Abdelfattah, who had told her about the olive trees of Palestine.

The Crown prosecutor, Mark Zarifeh, called Tarrant "clearly New Zealand's worst murderer" and said no minimum term was long enough. Kerry Cook, the lawyer assisting the court, argued against a whole-life term, citing Tarrant's age, lack of a previous record and guilty pleas, and said it would breach fundamental human rights; he also told the court that Tarrant's views had changed in jail and that he had offered to take part in restorative justice. Zarifeh questioned the sincerity of Tarrant's late description of his acts as "unnecessary, abhorrent and irrational".

Judge Cameron Mander found otherwise. In his remarks he said the evidence showed Tarrant held longstanding discriminatory views against ethnic minorities, rejected his claim that he had not targeted people for their religion or ethnicity, and said Tarrant was "empty of any empathy" for his victims. "Your crimes are so wicked," he said, "that even if you are detained until you die it will not exhaust the requirements of punishment and denunciation." Under the Sentencing Act, he explained, a whole-life term is available when no minimum period would satisfy the purposes of sentencing. He also accepted that Tarrant had given up the chance to use a trial as a platform when he pleaded guilty.

Temel Atacocugu, who was shot nine times at Al Noor, said the justice system had "locked up this ideology forever". The imam of Al Noor, Gamal Fouda, said no punishment would bring back the dead. Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern said she hoped it would be the last time anyone had to utter the gunman's name, and that he deserved "a lifetime of complete and utter silence".

The Royal Commission of Inquiry was set up to establish what state agencies, including police, knew about the attacker before 15 March, what they could have done to prevent it, and what they should do in future. Its report, "Ko tō tātou kāinga tēnei", ran to roughly 800 pages and was released on 8 December 2020, about 18 months after the inquiry began, according to Al Jazeera. It made 44 recommendations.

The commission concluded that no single piece of information available to agencies could have warned of an impending attack. Al Jazeera, summarising the report, said the signs were too fragmentary to establish grounds for immediate action. Among them were what the report called hallmarks of steroid overuse, and a firearm accident in July 2018 for which, Al Jazeera reported, he sought treatment at a Dunedin hospital whose officials did not alert police. Daniel Byman of the Brookings Institution, writing about the report, quoted the report as finding "no plausible way" he could have been detected "except by chance".

The report was nonetheless critical. Intelligence services had directed their effort mainly at the threat of Islamist extremism, and the commission took issue with what it called an inappropriate concentration of resources on other terrorism threats, which distracted from threats such as white supremacists. Byman, who compared the document to the 9/11 Commission, wrote that it identified several real lapses in firearms regulation. Authorities had also been criticised for failing to heed warnings from the Muslim community about rising hate crime.

Ardern apologised on behalf of the government. "While the commission made no findings that these issues would have stopped the attack," she said, "these were failings nonetheless." She added that the report came down to one premise, that Muslim New Zealanders should be safe. Al Jazeera reported that many in the Muslim community accepted the recommendations while some felt the report had said too little about how their concerns had been overlooked.
NPR reported that Ardern responded to the attack by banning semi-automatic weapons and starting a buyback for gun owners. Al Jazeera said the attacks also prompted changes to social media protocols.

The Labour government had promised to carry out all 44 recommendations. Five years after the attack, the coordinating minister, Collins, announced that the coordinated response had concluded. Of the 44, 36 had been implemented or folded into continuing work, and eight would not go ahead. Those included a new national intelligence and security agency, an advisory group on counter-terrorism, a public reporting system for concerning behaviour, and mandatory reporting of firearm injuries by health professionals. Two more, repealing section 131 of the Human Rights Act and widening the legal definition of "objectionable" material, were tied to hate speech law, which the coalition agreement between National and New Zealand First said would not change.

She listed outcomes such as the first National Security Strategy, a Firearms Safety Authority and a Ministry for Ethnic Communities. An annual broadcast of the call to prayer would continue and the government was considering a memorial to the shuhada, the martyrs. The Labour leader, Chris Hipkins, said "disappointing" was "not enough of a word" for the decision. Police separately received funding in July 2021 for a programme called Te Raranga, meant to improve their response to hate crime; between 1 January and 24 June 2021 police received 1,693 hate crime reports.
